questions.stem: Which statement best describes an indictable offence?
options: A minor offence that is generally heard and determined by a magistrate in the Magistrates' Court, without a jury
Any offence where the accused has decided to plead guilty before the case reaches a hearing
A civil wrong in which the person harmed sues the wrongdoer for compensation in a higher court
A serious offence that is generally heard before a judge and jury in the County Court or Supreme Court
questions.explanation: Indictable offences are the more serious crimes, such as armed robbery or murder, and a contested indictable offence is tried by a judge and jury in the County Court or Supreme Court. Minor offences heard by a magistrate are summary offences; the seriousness of the charge, not the plea, decides the category.

questions.stem: Jasmine is charged with careless driving after she drifts across a lane on the Monash Freeway. No-one is hurt. Which court will most likely hear her case, and why?
options: The Court of Appeal, because traffic matters skip the trial courts
The Magistrates' Court, because careless driving is a summary offence
The County Court, because all driving offences are indictable offences
The Supreme Court, because the offence happened on a major freeway
questions.explanation: Careless driving is a minor offence, so it is a summary offence heard and determined by a magistrate in the Magistrates' Court. Driving offences are not all indictable: only serious ones such as culpable driving causing death are, and those go to the County Court.

questions.stem: An accused charged with a less serious indictable offence agrees to have it heard in the Magistrates' Court, and the magistrate considers it appropriate. This is known as:
options: an indictable offence heard summarily
a committal hearing for a summary offence
a plea negotiation between the parties
a summary offence heard on indictment
questions.explanation: Some indictable offences may be heard and determined summarily in the Magistrates' Court if the accused consents and the court considers it appropriate. A committal hearing is a different step: it decides whether there is enough evidence for an indictable case to go to trial in a higher court.

questions.stem: In a Victorian criminal trial, the burden of proof rests with:
options: the judge, who must decide which evidence is presented
the jury, which must gather evidence about the offence
the prosecution, which must prove the accused is guilty
the accused, who must prove to the court that they are innocent
questions.explanation: The party that brings the case carries the burden of proof, and in a criminal case that is the prosecution. The accused does not have to prove innocence, because the presumption of innocence means guilt must be proved, not assumed.

questions.stem: The standard of proof in a criminal case is:
options: beyond any possible doubt at all
beyond reasonable doubt
on the balance of probabilities
on the strength of a prima facie case
questions.explanation: A jury or magistrate may find an accused guilty only if guilt is proved beyond reasonable doubt. The balance of probabilities is the lower civil standard, and the law does not demand proof beyond every possible doubt, which could never be met.

questions.stem: During a trial, the judge directs the jury that the accused has no obligation to explain anything and must be treated as innocent until proven guilty. Which principle is the judge upholding most directly?
options: The right to trial without delay
The principle of open justice
The right to be informed of charges
The presumption of innocence
questions.explanation: Treating the accused as innocent until guilt is proved is the presumption of innocence, which places the task of proof on the prosecution. Trial without unreasonable delay is a separate right concerned with how long a case takes to come to court.

questions.stem: Why is the criminal standard of proof set higher than the civil standard?
options: The prosecution has more resources than an accused, so the standard is raised to make trials run more quickly than civil cases
Juries in criminal cases are larger than civil juries, so they are able to apply a more demanding standard to the evidence
A conviction can lead to a loss of liberty and a criminal record, so the risk of convicting an innocent person must be kept low
Criminal cases are heard in higher courts than civil cases, so they must always meet the stricter standard used in those courts
questions.explanation: The higher standard reflects the serious consequences of a guilty verdict, including imprisonment and the stigma of a conviction. The level of court has nothing to do with it: a summary offence in the Magistrates' Court must still be proved beyond reasonable doubt.

questions.stem: Under the right to silence, an accused person in Victoria:
options: generally does not have to answer police questions or give evidence at their own trial
may refuse to plead to the charge, and the court must then dismiss the case against them
cannot be asked by police for any details, including their name and their home address
can stop prosecution witnesses from giving evidence about anything the accused has said
questions.explanation: The right to silence means an accused need not answer police questions or give evidence at trial, and the jury must not treat that silence as a sign of guilt. It is not absolute, though: police can require a name and address in some circumstances.

questions.stem: Theo was charged with an indictable offence and has waited almost three years for his trial because of a backlog in the County Court. Which right of the accused is most at risk?
options: The right to trial by jury for indictable offences
The right to be informed of the offender's release
The right to be tried without unreasonable delay
The right to silence during police questioning
questions.explanation: Long delays can cause stress, keep an accused on remand and weaken evidence as memories fade, so the Charter protects the right to be tried without unreasonable delay. The right to be informed of an offender's release date is a victim's right, not one held by the accused.

questions.stem: Which statement about the right to trial by jury in Victoria is correct?
options: An accused who pleads not guilty to an indictable offence is tried before a jury
An accused who pleads not guilty to a summary offence may choose to have a jury trial
Every accused who pleads guilty is sentenced by a jury in the County Court
A jury decides guilt in criminal cases heard in the Magistrates' Court
questions.explanation: Juries decide guilt in trials of indictable offences where the accused pleads not guilty. There are no juries in the Magistrates' Court, and an accused who pleads guilty is sentenced by the judge, so a jury plays no part.

questions.stem: Section 80 of the Australian Constitution protects trial by jury, yet a person charged with a serious Victorian offence relies on state legislation for a jury. Why?
options: Section 80 applies only to criminal trials that are heard in the High Court of Australia
Section 80 applies only to trials on indictment for offences against Commonwealth laws
Section 80 applies only to summary offences heard in the Magistrates' Court
Section 80 was repealed at a referendum and replaced by state jury laws
questions.explanation: Section 80 guarantees a jury for trials on indictment of Commonwealth offences only, so it does not cover offences against Victorian law. Victorian juries come from state laws such as the Juries Act 2000 (Vic); section 80 has never been changed by referendum.

questions.stem: In Victoria, the rights of victims of crime are set out mainly in the:
options: Sentencing Act 1991 (Vic) alone
Victims' Charter Act 2006 (Vic)
Australian Constitution, Chapter III
Civil Procedure Act 2010 (Vic)
questions.explanation: The Victims' Charter Act 2006 (Vic) sets out how investigatory, prosecuting and victims' services agencies must treat victims, including keeping them informed. Chapter III of the Constitution concerns the federal judicature and contains no list of victims' rights.

questions.stem: Mia, aged 15, is the complainant in a sexual offence trial. She gives her evidence from a separate room by closed-circuit television so she does not have to face the accused. This is an example of:
options: the right to make a victim impact statement to the court
the right to give evidence using alternative arrangements
the right to be informed about the proceedings
the right to silence as it applies to a witness
questions.explanation: Alternative arrangements, such as giving evidence by CCTV, using screens or having a support person nearby, reduce the trauma of giving evidence for vulnerable witnesses. A victim impact statement is used at sentencing, not while the victim gives evidence at trial.

questions.stem: A man convicted of assault is serving a prison sentence. His victim registers so that she can find out when he is likely to be released. Which right of victims is she using?
options: The right to give evidence using alternative arrangements
The right to be consulted about any plea negotiation that takes place
The right to be informed of the likely release date of the offender
The right to be informed about the progress of the prosecution
questions.explanation: Eligible victims can join the Victims Register to be told of an offender's likely release date, which helps them plan for their safety. The right to be informed about the prosecution covers the charges and court process, which end once the sentence is imposed.

questions.stem: In VCE Legal Studies, the principle of equality means that:
options: every person should have a fair hearing before an impartial decision-maker, using processes that are open and transparent to public scrutiny and comment
every person should be able to engage with the justice system and its processes on an informed basis, and understand their rights
people should be treated in the same way, and where that would disadvantage someone, measures should allow them to take part without disadvantage
every person should receive exactly the same outcome in their case, whatever the circumstances of the offence that they committed
questions.explanation: Equality means treating people the same way and, where identical treatment would disadvantage someone, using measures such as an interpreter so they can take part on equal terms. Open and impartial processes describe fairness, and informed engagement describes access.

questions.stem: A Mandarin-speaking accused is given a free interpreter for her trial so she can follow the evidence. Which principle of justice does this most directly promote?
options: Deterrence
Denunciation
Supremacy
Equality
questions.explanation: Providing an interpreter is a measure that removes a disadvantage so she can engage with the trial on the same basis as an English speaker, which is equality. Deterrence and denunciation are purposes of sanctions, not principles of justice.

questions.stem: The Victorian Supreme Court publishes its judgments online and most trials are open to the public. Which principle of justice does this most directly support?
options: Equality, through free legal advice
Fairness, through open processes
Equality, through equal outcomes
Access, through cheaper legal fees
questions.explanation: Fairness includes having processes that are open and impartial, so the public can see justice being done. Publishing judgments does not lower anyone's legal fees, and equality is about equal treatment, not identical outcomes.

questions.stem: Kai lives in a remote part of Gippsland, cannot afford a lawyer and does not know that free legal information is available online. Which principle of justice is most clearly not being achieved, and why?
options: Equality, because the law treats Kai differently from people in Melbourne
Fairness, because Kai has been denied the presumption of innocence by police
Access, because Kai cannot engage with the justice system on an informed basis
Fairness, because the court hearing Kai's case will not be impartial or open
questions.explanation: Access is about being able to engage with the justice system and its processes on an informed basis, and Kai lacks both information and help. Nothing suggests the court itself is biased or closed, so fairness is not the main concern here.

questions.stem: Which service does Victoria Legal Aid provide to people facing criminal charges?
options: Final decisions about which accused should be granted or refused bail
Duty lawyers at courts and grants of legal assistance for eligible people
Free representation in court for every accused, whatever their income or charge
Investigation of crimes and the laying of charges against offenders
questions.explanation: Victoria Legal Aid provides free legal information, duty lawyers at court and grants of legal assistance to people who meet its means test and guidelines. It does not fund everyone, and investigating crime and deciding bail are the jobs of police and the courts.

questions.stem: Elif earns a moderate wage and was refused a grant of legal assistance by Victoria Legal Aid for her County Court trial. What is the most likely reason?
options: Victoria Legal Aid is not permitted to assist with criminal cases
Grants of legal assistance are available only to victims of crime
Victoria Legal Aid funds only cases heard in the High Court
She did not meet the means test or the guidelines for a grant
questions.explanation: Grants of legal assistance are limited by a means test, a merits test and guidelines, so a person on a moderate income can miss out yet still be unable to afford a private lawyer. Victoria Legal Aid does a great deal of criminal work; it is limited by funding, not barred from criminal law.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the role of Victorian community legal centres?
options: Government bodies that prosecute summary offences on behalf of Victoria Police in local courts
Private law firms that act only for wealthy clients in major indictable trials in the higher courts
Courts that hear minor criminal cases in local communities instead of the Magistrates' Court
Independent non-profit bodies that give free legal advice, casework and community legal education
questions.explanation: Community legal centres are independent, non-profit organisations that provide free legal advice, some casework and community legal education, and some specialise in areas such as family violence. They rarely run long indictable trials, which is mainly work for Victoria Legal Aid and private lawyers.

questions.stem: Plea negotiations are:
options: discussions between the magistrate and the police about whether an accused should be granted bail
pre-trial discussions between the prosecution and the accused about the charges the accused will plead guilty to
discussions between the judge and the jury, held before the verdict, about the sentence that should be imposed on the accused
meetings between the victim and the accused, run by a mediator, to agree on the amount of compensation
questions.explanation: Plea negotiations happen before trial between the prosecution and the accused, usually through their lawyers, and often end with the accused pleading guilty to fewer or lesser charges. The judge takes no part, and the outcome is a plea, not an agreed sentence.

questions.stem: Raj is charged with intentionally causing serious injury. After plea negotiations, he pleads guilty to the lesser charge of recklessly causing serious injury. Which is the most likely benefit for the justice system?
options: The jury can deliver its verdict more quickly because the charge is now less serious
The victim gains the right to decide the sentence because Raj has admitted his guilt
A trial is avoided, saving court time and costs and sparing the victim from giving evidence
Raj is guaranteed a non-custodial sentence because the prosecution has accepted his plea
questions.explanation: A guilty plea removes the need for a trial, which saves time and money and spares the victim the stress of testifying. The plea does not guarantee any sentence: the judge still decides it, and there is no jury once an accused pleads guilty.

questions.stem: A victim feels that a plea negotiation has let the offender plead to a charge that does not reflect what happened. Which statement best explains why this criticism arises?
options: Negotiations happen in private and the victim's views must be considered, but the victim cannot veto the agreement
Negotiations are run by the trial judge, who then has to accept whatever charge the accused offers to plead guilty to
Negotiations allow the accused to set their own sentence, which the court is then bound to impose
Negotiations take place in open court, so the victim is pressured to agree in front of the jury
questions.explanation: Plea negotiations take place privately between the parties, and although the prosecution must consider the victim's views, the victim does not decide the outcome. The judge is not part of the negotiation and the sentence remains for the court to decide.

questions.stem: Which Victorian court hears trials for murder and attempted murder?
options: The Supreme Court (Trial Division)
The County Court of Victoria
The Magistrates' Court of Victoria
The Supreme Court (Court of Appeal)
questions.explanation: The most serious indictable offences, including murder, attempted murder and treason, are tried in the Trial Division of the Supreme Court. The Court of Appeal hears appeals rather than trials, and the County Court handles most other indictable offences.

questions.stem: The Drug Court and the Koori Court are divisions within the court hierarchy. Which reason for the court hierarchy do they best illustrate?
options: Precedent, because their decisions bind every other court in the hierarchy
Administrative convenience, because they share their judges with the High Court of Australia
Specialisation, because courts can develop expertise in particular types of cases
Appeals, because they review decisions made by the County and Supreme Courts
questions.explanation: Specialist divisions let courts build expertise and adopt procedures suited to particular offenders and offences, which is specialisation. Neither the Drug Court nor the Koori Court is an appeal court, and neither shares judges with the High Court.

questions.stem: Nadia is convicted in the County Court and believes the judge made an error of law. To which court would she appeal?
options: The Magistrates' Court of Victoria
The Trial Division of the Supreme Court
The Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal
The Court of Appeal of the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: Criminal appeals from the County Court go to the Court of Appeal, which can review the trial and correct errors. The Trial Division hears trials and some appeals from the Magistrates' Court, not appeals from the County Court.

questions.stem: Why does the existence of appeals within the court hierarchy best promote fairness?
options: Appeals let the victim choose a different judge if they disagree with the original sentence
Appeals mean that juries in the lower courts do not need to reach a unanimous verdict
A higher court with more experienced judges can correct mistakes made in a lower court
Every accused gets an automatic second trial in a higher court if they are unhappy with the verdict
questions.explanation: The hierarchy allows mistakes of law, fact or sentence to be corrected by a higher court, which helps ensure a fair process and outcome. Appeals are not automatic: there must be grounds, and in many cases leave to appeal is needed.

questions.stem: In a Victorian criminal jury trial, the jury:
options: decides which evidence is admissible before the trial begins
decides the charges that the prosecution should proceed with
decides whether the accused is guilty or not guilty on the evidence
decides the sentence after the accused has been found guilty
questions.explanation: The jury's role is to weigh the evidence and deliver a verdict of guilty or not guilty. Sentencing and rulings on whether evidence is admissible belong to the judge, and charges are chosen by the prosecution.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a role of the judge in a criminal jury trial?
options: Questioning witnesses closely to find out the truth and deciding the verdict alongside the jury
Presenting evidence to the court on behalf of the prosecution to prove the accused is guilty
Advising the accused on whether to plead guilty and on which witnesses they should call
Explaining the relevant law to the jury and imposing a sentence if the accused is found guilty
questions.explanation: The judge acts as an impartial umpire: they rule on evidence, give the jury directions on the law and sentence the offender if there is a guilty verdict. Presenting evidence and advising the accused are tasks for the parties and their lawyers.

questions.stem: Victoria uses an adversarial system. Which statement best explains how the parties' roles in a criminal trial reflect this?
options: Each party prepares and presents its own case and tests the other's evidence before a passive judge
The judge leads the investigation and the parties answer the judge's questions about the evidence
The jury questions each party directly and then reaches its verdict together with the judge
The parties agree on the facts in advance and the judge then decides which party's story to prefer
questions.explanation: In the adversarial system, the prosecution and the defence each run their own case, call and cross-examine witnesses, and the judge stays a neutral umpire. A judge who leads the investigation is a feature of an inquisitorial system, not Victoria's.

questions.stem: Why is an accused in a serious criminal trial likely to need a legal practitioner?
options: Lawyers understand the rules of evidence and procedure and can present the case objectively
Only lawyers are permitted to speak in a courtroom, so an accused cannot represent themselves
Juries are required to disregard any evidence that the accused personally puts to the court
The prosecution is not permitted to proceed with a trial until the accused has a lawyer
questions.explanation: Criminal trials involve complex rules of evidence and procedure, and a lawyer can test the prosecution's case, present the defence and stay objective under pressure. People can represent themselves, which is exactly why doing so carries a risk of unfairness.

questions.stem: In Dietrich v The Queen (1992), the High Court found that where an accused charged with a serious offence cannot obtain legal representation through no fault of their own:
options: the trial should ordinarily be adjourned or stayed until representation is available, as it may otherwise be unfair
the state must always provide a free private barrister of the accused's own choosing for the full length of the trial
the accused must represent themselves, but the judge must then act as their lawyer during the trial
the charges must be withdrawn permanently, because the accused can never receive a fair trial
questions.explanation: Dietrich established that a trial of a serious offence without representation may be unfair, so a judge should ordinarily adjourn or stay it until the accused is represented. It did not create a right to a free lawyer of one's choice, and the charges are not dropped for good.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains how cultural differences can limit the achievement of justice for an accused?
options: Cultural differences require the prosecution to meet a lower standard of proof against the accused
A language barrier or unfamiliarity with the system may stop an accused from understanding the case against them
Cultural differences mean an accused may be tried under a different set of criminal laws from other Victorians
Cultural differences mean an accused must be tried by a jury drawn only from their own cultural community
questions.explanation: Language barriers, distrust of authorities and unfamiliar processes can prevent an accused from understanding or participating, which affects fairness and access. The same criminal laws and standard of proof apply to everyone, so the other options misstate the law.

questions.stem: The Koori Court sentences Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander offenders who plead guilty, with Elders or Respected Persons taking part. How does this most directly respond to cultural differences?
options: It allows a First Nations accused to contest their guilt before a jury made up only of Elders
It replaces the sentencing judge or magistrate with Elders, who then decide the sentence themselves
It makes sentencing more culturally relevant, which can reduce feelings of alienation and improve participation
It applies a separate set of criminal laws to First Nations accused, which is said to ensure equality before the law
questions.explanation: The Koori Court has a less formal setting and involves Elders and Respected Persons, which can make the process more meaningful and help offenders engage. The judicial officer still imposes the sentence under the same law, and the Koori Court deals only with accused who plead guilty.

questions.stem: Which purpose of sanctions aims to discourage other people in the community from committing similar offences?
options: Rehabilitation
Denunciation
General deterrence
Specific deterrence
questions.explanation: General deterrence aims to discourage the wider community from offending by showing the consequences. Specific deterrence targets the individual offender, discouraging them from reoffending.

questions.stem: In sentencing a man for a violent assault on a paramedic, the judge says the community strongly condemns attacks on emergency workers. Which purpose of sanctions is the judge emphasising?
options: Denunciation
Rehabilitation
Protection
Specific deterrence
questions.explanation: Denunciation is the court expressing, on behalf of the community, its disapproval of the offender's conduct. Protection would focus on keeping the community safe from this offender, which the judge's remark does not mention.

questions.stem: Lena, aged 19, pleads guilty to burglary committed to fund a drug addiction. The court imposes a community correction order with conditions of drug treatment and supervision. Which purpose does this sanction most directly aim to achieve?
options: Denunciation
General deterrence
Protection
Rehabilitation
questions.explanation: Treatment and supervision conditions address the cause of Lena's offending, so the main aim is rehabilitation. A community correction order can also punish and protect, but a treatment-focused order is aimed first at changing her behaviour.

questions.stem: Which statement about a community correction order is correct?
options: It is served in the community and has mandatory conditions as well as at least one optional condition
It is served in a prison and is reserved for offenders who have committed the most serious crimes
It is a monetary penalty paid to the court, which the offender may be allowed to pay in instalments over time
It is an order the victim applies for, requiring the offender to pay compensation to the victim
questions.explanation: A community correction order is a non-custodial sanction with mandatory conditions, such as not reoffending, plus at least one optional condition, such as unpaid community work or treatment. A monetary penalty is a fine, which is a separate sanction.

questions.stem: Which purpose is a fine best suited to achieve for a minor offence?
options: Denunciation, by placing the offender under supervision
Punishment and deterrence, by imposing a financial burden
Protection, by removing the offender from the community
Rehabilitation, by treating the cause of the offending
questions.explanation: A fine punishes by taking money and deters the offender and others from repeating the offence. It does not remove the offender from society or address the cause of offending, so it does little for protection or rehabilitation.

questions.stem: Under Victorian sentencing law, imprisonment is described as a sanction of last resort. This means a court should:
options: imprison an offender only once the victim has consented to a custodial sentence being imposed
only imprison an offender who has been found guilty of an offence after a full trial before a jury
not imprison an offender unless the purposes of sentencing cannot be achieved by a less severe sanction
only imprison an offender if they have already served a community correction order for the same offence
questions.explanation: The Sentencing Act 1991 (Vic) says a court must not impose imprisonment unless the purposes of sentencing cannot be achieved by a less severe sentence. Prison does not require a prior order or the victim's consent, and offenders who plead guilty can still be imprisoned.

questions.stem: A critic argues that imprisonment often fails to achieve specific deterrence. Which evidence would best support this view?
options: Judges are able to express the community's disapproval when imposing a prison sentence
A high proportion of released prisoners return to prison within a few years of release
Prison sentences are reported in the media and so are seen by many members of the public
Prisoners are kept away from the community for the length of their custodial sentence
questions.explanation: Specific deterrence aims to stop the individual offender from reoffending, so high rates of return to prison suggest it is not working. Media reporting relates to general deterrence, and removal from the community relates to protection.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an aggravating factor in sentencing?
options: The offender showed genuine remorse for the offence in court
The offender had no prior criminal convictions
The offender cooperated fully with the police
The offender used a weapon and the victim was elderly
questions.explanation: Aggravating factors make an offence more serious and can increase the sentence, such as using a weapon or targeting a vulnerable victim. Remorse, a clean record and cooperation with police are mitigating factors that can reduce it.

questions.stem: When an offender pleads guilty in Victoria, the court may reduce the sentence and must state the sentence it would have imposed without the plea. Which is the main reason a guilty plea attracts a reduction?
options: It saves the time and cost of a trial and spares victims and witnesses from giving evidence
It proves the offender is not guilty of the more serious charge the prosecution first laid
It means the court does not need to consider any aggravating factors present in the case
It allows the jury to recommend a lighter sentence to the judge at the close of the trial
questions.explanation: A guilty plea saves court resources and spares victims the trauma of a trial, and it can also show remorse, so it is rewarded with a sentencing discount. Aggravating factors are still taken into account, and there is no jury involved after a guilty plea.

questions.stem: Which statement about a victim impact statement is correct?
options: It describes the effect of the crime on the victim and is considered by the court when sentencing
It is used by the jury to help it decide whether the accused is guilty or not guilty of the offence
It is a statement that the victim gives to police before charges are laid against the accused
It sets the sentence that the court must impose on the offender after a guilty verdict
questions.explanation: A victim impact statement explains how the offence has affected the victim, physically, emotionally or financially, and the court takes it into account in sentencing. It is not used to decide guilt, and the judge, not the victim, decides the sentence.
